module.title: Python for AI
module.subtitle: The practical Python subset you need before models, APIs and data pipelines.
module.description: A focused Python module for AI work: data structures, typed functions, NumPy and pandas, API calls, errors and tests. It skips web frameworks and language trivia, and ends with a real notes-to-dataset pipeline.
outcomes: Turn lists, dictionaries and JSON into clean, predictable AI data structures.
Write typed functions and small modules with tests instead of fragile notebooks.
Load, clean and summarise tabular data with pandas and vectorised NumPy operations.
Call an AI API safely with environment secrets, timeouts, retries and error handling.

lessons.title: The Python data toolkit for AI
lessons.summary: Lists, dictionaries, sets, comprehensions, JSON and generators — the shapes AI data actually takes.
lessons.body_html:
Most AI code is data plumbing. Before a model sees anything, a list becomes a DataFrame, a JSON response becomes a dictionary, and a document becomes a stream of chunks. Choose the right structure and the rest gets simpler.

Four containers, four jobs

  • List — ordered, mutable, duplicates allowed. Use it for batches, messages and predictions.
  • Dictionary — keyed lookup. Use it for records, JSON objects and configuration.
  • Tuple — ordered and immutable. Use it for fixed groups such as (input, label).
  • Set — unique values. Use it for vocabularies, IDs and deduplication.
record = {"text": "reset my password", "label": "account"}
labels = {"billing", "bug", "account"}
batch = [record, {"text": "charged twice", "label": "billing"}]

for item in batch:
    print(item["text"], "→", item["label"])

Comprehensions: transform a batch

texts = [item["text"].lower() for item in batch]
lengths = {item["label"]: len(item["text"]) for item in batch}
unique_labels = {item["label"] for item in batch}

Comprehensions are fine for a single readable transformation. If the logic needs branches and comments, use a normal loop instead of a dense one-liner.

JSON is a dictionary with rules

import json

payload = json.loads('{"question": "What is RAG?"}')
encoded = json.dumps({"answer": "Retrieval-augmented generation"}, ensure_ascii=False)

with open("sessions.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    json.dump({"sessions": []}, handle, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

JSON objects map to dictionaries, arrays to lists, strings to strings, and numbers to numbers. Always pass a file encoding and decide explicitly how to handle invalid JSON.

Generators for large data

def read_lines(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            yield line.strip()

A generator produces one item at a time instead of loading everything into memory. That matters when you process a large notes file, log export or document corpus.

AI habit: keep raw data immutable. Build new lists and dictionaries with comprehensions instead of mutating a shared record inside a loop.

Worked example: an API response into training records

response = {
    "items": [
        {"id": 1, "text": "Reset my password", "labels": ["account"]},
        {"id": 2, "text": "Charged twice", "labels": ["billing"]},
        {"id": 3, "text": "App crashes on upload", "labels": ["bug"]},
    ]
}

records = [
    {
        "id": item["id"],
        "text": " ".join(item["text"].lower().split()),
        "label": item["labels"][0] if item["labels"] else "unlabelled",
    }
    for item in response["items"]
]

This is the shape of most AI data preparation: reach into a nested response, keep the fields you need, normalise text, and produce a flat list of records. The transformation is explicit and easy to test because it has no hidden global state.

Sets for deduplication

seen = set()
unique = []
for record in records:
    key = record["text"]
    if key not in seen:
        seen.add(key)
        unique.append(record)

Sets give O(1) membership checks. This is much faster than scanning a list with if key not in list for every record. Order is not preserved by the set itself, so keep a separate list when output order matters.

Common mistakes

  • Using record.text on a dictionary. Use record["text"] unless you have converted it to a dataclass or object.
  • Mutating a list while iterating over it. Build a new list instead.
  • Loading a huge JSON file into a list when a line-delimited stream would work. Prefer JSONL for large exports.
  • Assuming all items have the same keys. Use .get() with a deliberate default, or validate the schema.
Extra practice: write a function that accepts the API response and returns a dictionary keyed by record id. Then write a second function that converts the same response into JSONL. Success: both functions work on a response with a missing labels field.
takeaways: Lists, dicts, tuples and sets have different jobs; choose by behaviour, not habit.
JSON maps naturally to dictionaries and lists, but needs explicit encoding and error handling.
Generators keep large files and corpora memory-friendly.
lessons.practice: Take a JSON list of 20 notes and produce: a list of lowercase texts, a set of unique labels, and a dictionary counting labels. Success: no nested loop longer than three lines and no mutation of the original records.

lessons.title: Functions, typing and a project that survives
lessons.summary: Small typed functions, dataclasses, virtual environments and tests — the difference between a notebook and a tool.
lessons.body_html:
AI experiments rot quickly when everything lives in one notebook cell. A small project with clear functions can be tested, reused in a CLI, and deployed behind an API.

Functions with explicit contracts

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Note:
    text: str
    label: str

def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(text.strip().lower().split())

def to_note(raw: dict) -> Note:
    return Note(
        text=clean_text(raw.get("text", "")),
        label=raw.get("label", "unlabelled"),
    )

A typed function documents its inputs and output. Python does not enforce the types at runtime, but tests, editors and mypy can catch mistakes before a model run.

Defaults, keyword arguments and *args

def chunk_text(text: str, size: int = 500, overlap: int = 50) -> list[str]:
    if size <= overlap:
        raise ValueError("size must be greater than overlap")
    step = size - overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

Keyword arguments make call sites readable: chunk_text(text, size=800, overlap=80). Validate impossible combinations early instead of debugging them deep in a model call.

A project shape that scales

notes_ai/
  pyproject.toml
  requirements.txt
  src/notes_ai/
    __init__.py
    data.py
    pipeline.py
    cli.py
  tests/
    test_pipeline.py

Use a virtual environment and pin dependencies. Keep notebooks in a separate notebooks/ folder for exploration. The code that produces results belongs in src/; the code that proves it works belongs in tests/.

Test the contract, not the implementation

def test_chunk_text_rejects_bad_overlap():
    try:
        chunk_text("abc", size=10, overlap=10)
    except ValueError:
        return
    raise AssertionError("expected ValueError")

Good tests describe behaviour: what happens with empty input, a bad parameter, a missing key, or a provider timeout. That is how a notebook becomes a tool.

Minimum viable structure: one virtual environment, pinned dependencies, a src/ package, a tests/ folder, and a README that says how to run both.

Worked example: a typed configuration object

import os
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    model: str
    timeout_seconds: int
    max_retries: int

    @classmethod
    def from_env(cls) -> "Settings":
        return cls(
            model=os.environ.get("LLM_MODEL", "small-model"),
            timeout_seconds=int(os.environ.get("LLM_TIMEOUT", "30")),
            max_retries=int(os.environ.get("LLM_RETRIES", "2")),
        )

A frozen dataclass gives you a small, named configuration object instead of passing five loose strings around. from_env keeps environment parsing in one place, which makes tests easy: set the variables, construct settings, assert the fields.

Worked example: a pytest test with a fake

from notes_ai.pipeline import clean_text

def test_clean_text_collapses_whitespace():
    assert clean_text("  Reset   Password  ") == "reset password"

def test_clean_text_handles_empty_input():
    assert clean_text("   ") == ""

Tests should describe behaviour, not restate the implementation. Name the condition and the expected result. If a test needs a network call or a paid API, replace that dependency with a fake in the test.

Common mistakes

  • Mutable default arguments. def f(items=[]) reuses the same list across calls; use None and create a new list inside.
  • Bare except:. It hides programming errors and cancellation. Catch the specific exception you can handle.
  • Secrets in source or notebooks. Read them from the environment and keep a placeholder in .env.example.
  • No project boundary. One importable package with a CLI entry point is easier to test than a hundred notebook cells.
Extra practice: add a --dry-run flag to a CLI that prints what it would write without touching the filesystem. Test it with a temporary directory.
takeaways: Typed functions and dataclasses make data contracts visible.
Validate impossible arguments at the boundary, not deep inside a pipeline.
A virtual environment, pinned dependencies and tests turn a notebook into a tool.
lessons.practice: Turn one messy notebook cell into a typed function with a docstring and two tests: one happy path and one invalid input. Success: the tests run without a model call.

lessons.title: NumPy and pandas for AI data
lessons.summary: Arrays, vectorisation, DataFrames, missing values and a clean train/validation split.
lessons.body_html:
NumPy and pandas are the default tools for tabular and numeric data. The goal is not to memorise every method; it is to stop writing Python loops for operations that already exist and are tested.

NumPy: arrays and vectorisation

import numpy as np

scores = np.array([0.2, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4])
labels = scores >= 0.5
print(labels)                 # [False  True  True False]
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())

Vectorised operations run in compiled code and express intent clearly. Broadcasting lets you combine arrays of compatible shapes without manual loops. If you are writing a Python loop over a million numbers, check for a vectorised version first.

DataFrames are tables with labels

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("notes.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head())

clean = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["text"]).copy()
clean["text"] = clean["text"].str.strip().str.lower()
clean["label"] = clean["label"].fillna("unlabelled")

Inspect shape, types and missingness before modelling. A column that looks numeric may be stored as text because of one bad row.

Grouping and summaries

summary = (
    clean.groupby("label")
    .agg(rows=("text", "size"), avg_length=("text", lambda s: s.str.len().mean()))
    .sort_values("rows", ascending=False)
)
print(summary)

Slice analysis starts here: overall averages hide which classes, customers or time periods are failing.

Split without leakage

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train, valid = train_test_split(
    clean, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=clean["label"]
)
train.to_csv("train.csv", index=False)
valid.to_csv("valid.csv", index=False)

For time-dependent data, split by time instead of randomly. For grouped data, split by customer or document. The split must match how the model will be used.

Pipeline habit: save the raw file, the cleaned file and the split script. If you cannot reproduce the split, you cannot trust the score.

Worked example: a five-minute data audit

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("notes.csv")
print("rows:", len(df))
print("columns:", list(df.columns))
print("missing:\n", df.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head())
print("duplicate texts:", df["text"].duplicated().sum())
print("labels:\n", df["label"].value_counts(dropna=False))

This audit catches the failures that make a model look better or worse than it is: duplicated rows, a dominant class, missing labels, and columns with unexpected types. Run it before every experiment.

Filtering and assigning safely

clean = df.dropna(subset=["text"]).copy()
clean["text"] = clean["text"].str.strip().str.lower()
short = clean[clean["text"].str.len() >= 10]
billing = clean[clean["label"].eq("billing")]

Use .copy() when you intend to modify a filtered table. Chained assignment such as df[df.label == "bug"]["text"] = ... is unpredictable and often does not update the original DataFrame.

Merging metadata

labels = pd.read_csv("label_guide.csv")  # columns: label, description
enriched = clean.merge(labels, on="label", how="left", validate="many_to_one")

validate makes the expected cardinality explicit. If the label guide accidentally contains duplicate labels, the merge fails instead of silently multiplying rows.

Common mistakes

  • Computing statistics before the split. Means, target rates and scalers must come from training data only.
  • Forgetting .copy() before modifying a filtered frame. You may mutate a view or trigger a warning.
  • Ignoring the label distribution. A random split can produce a validation set with almost no rare examples.
  • Using a Python loop over a column. Use .str, .map, .apply or vectorised NumPy operations first.
Extra practice: add a column with text length, group by label, and report count, mean length and missing-text rate. Then check whether the split preserved the label ratio.
takeaways: Vectorised NumPy operations replace slow Python loops and make intent clear.
Always inspect shape, types, duplicates and missing values before modelling.
The split must match deployment: random, temporal or grouped.
lessons.practice: Load a CSV into pandas, clean text and labels, print a label summary, and save a stratified train/validation split. Success: rerunning the script produces the same row counts.

lessons.title: APIs, secrets and error handling
lessons.summary: Call an AI provider without leaking keys, hanging forever, or crashing on a bad response.
lessons.body_html:
Most AI applications are a thin Python layer around external APIs. That layer must handle slow providers, invalid JSON, rate limits and missing credentials without exposing secrets or hanging the user.

Read secrets from the environment

import os

api_key = os.environ.get("LLM_API_KEY")
if not api_key:
    raise RuntimeError("Set LLM_API_KEY before running this command")

Never commit a key. Do not put it in a notebook output, a README or a prompt. Commit a .env.example with placeholders, and keep the real file out of version control.

Every external call needs a timeout

import requests

def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.example.com/v1/chat",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
        json={"prompt": prompt},
        timeout=30,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    data = response.json()
    return data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

A timeout bounds latency and frees workers. Catch provider errors, decide whether the operation is safe to retry, and return a useful fallback or error to the caller.

Do not retry blindly

for attempt in range(3):
    try:
        return ask(prompt)
    except requests.Timeout:
        if attempt == 2:
            raise
        time.sleep(2 ** attempt)

Retries are for transient failures. A 400 invalid request will not fix itself. Writes need an idempotency key so a retry does not create a duplicate.

Async is not automatically faster

async/await helps when you have many independent I/O-bound calls. It does not speed up CPU-bound model preprocessing. Start synchronous, measure, and introduce concurrency only when the bottleneck is waiting on the network.

Test with a fake provider

def test_ask_uses_a_successful_response(monkeypatch):
    class FakeResponse:
        def raise_for_status(self): pass
        def json(self): return {"choices": [{"message": {"content": "ok"}}]}

    monkeypatch.setattr(requests, "post", lambda *a, **k: FakeResponse())
    assert ask("hello") == "ok"

Mocking the provider keeps tests fast, free and deterministic. Keep one small live smoke test separate from the unit suite.

Production minimum: secret from env, timeout, status check, structured error, bounded retry, and a test with a fake response.

Worked example: a small provider client

import json
import os
import time
import requests

class ProviderError(RuntimeError):
    pass

def ask_llm(prompt: str, retries: int = 2) -> str:
    key = os.environ.get("LLM_API_KEY")
    if not key:
        raise ProviderError("LLM_API_KEY is not configured")

    for attempt in range(retries + 1):
        try:
            response = requests.post(
                "https://api.example.com/v1/chat",
                headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
                json={"prompt": prompt},
                timeout=20,
            )
            if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < retries:
                time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
                continue
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
        except requests.Timeout:
            if attempt == retries:
                raise ProviderError("The provider timed out") from None
        except (KeyError, json.JSONDecodeError) as exc:
            raise ProviderError("Malformed provider response") from exc
    raise ProviderError("Provider request failed")

This is deliberately explicit: missing key, rate limit, timeout, malformed JSON and an exhausted retry budget all have a named failure path. A caller can catch ProviderError and show a useful message instead of a stack trace.

Async for independent calls

import asyncio
import httpx

async def fetch_one(client, prompt):
    response = await client.post("/v1/chat", json={"prompt": prompt}, timeout=20)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

async def fetch_many(prompts):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://api.example.com") as client:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_one(client, p) for p in prompts))

Concurrency helps when you have many independent network calls. It does not help CPU-bound preprocessing, and it makes rate limits easier to hit. Add a semaphore or a queue before you increase concurrency.

Common mistakes

  • No timeout. A slow provider can hold workers forever.
  • Retrying a 400/401. Invalid requests and auth failures will not fix themselves; surface them.
  • Logging the authorization header or full prompt. Log identifiers, status and latency, not secrets or sensitive data.
  • Testing against the live API. Use fakes for unit tests and keep a tiny, optional smoke test.
Extra practice: add a fake transport that returns 429 once and then succeeds. Assert that the client retried exactly once and returned the answer.
takeaways: Secrets belong in environment variables, never in source or prompts.
Every external call needs a timeout, status check and explicit failure path.
Retry only transient, idempotent operations; mock the provider in tests.
lessons.practice: Write a function that calls a fake LLM endpoint with a 5-second timeout, checks the status, parses JSON, and raises a clear error when the key is missing. Success: a test covers success and malformed JSON without network access.

lessons.title: Put it together: the notes pipeline
lessons.summary: A complete, runnable pipeline from raw JSONL notes to clean train/validation artifacts and a summary.
takeaways: A pipeline is a sequence of small, testable transformations with explicit inputs and outputs.
Write artifacts and a summary so another person can reproduce and inspect the dataset.
Tests should cover empty files, malformed records, deduplication and split determinism.
lessons.practice: Run the pipeline on five fake notes, then break one record on purpose and add a test that proves the bad record is rejected. Success: the error names the file and record, not just 'invalid data'.
lessons.body_html:
This lesson connects the previous four into one small project. The goal is not a clever algorithm; it is a pipeline a teammate can run twice and get the same result.

The shape

raw/*.jsonl → load → clean → deduplicate → split → artifacts
                                              ├── train.jsonl
                                              ├── valid.jsonl
                                              └── summary.json

1. Load JSONL safely

import json
from pathlib import Path

def read_jsonl(path: Path) -> list[dict]:
    records = []
    with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line_number, line in enumerate(handle, start=1):
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            try:
                item = json.loads(line)
            except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
                raise ValueError(f"{path}:{line_number}: invalid JSON") from exc
            if not isinstance(item, dict):
                raise ValueError(f"{path}:{line_number}: record must be an object")
            records.append(item)
    return records

JSONL is friendly for large exports: one record per line, appendable, and streamable. The error message includes the file and line number, which is the difference between a five-minute fix and an hour of guessing.

2. Clean and deduplicate

def clean_record(raw: dict) -> dict:
    text = " ".join(str(raw.get("text", "")).strip().lower().split())
    label = str(raw.get("label") or "unlabelled").strip().lower()
    return {"text": text, "label": label}

def clean_records(records: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    cleaned = []
    seen = set()
    for raw in records:
        record = clean_record(raw)
        if not record["text"] or record["text"] in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(record["text"])
        cleaned.append(record)
    return cleaned

Cleaning returns new dictionaries, drops empty text, and deduplicates by normalized text. The input is not mutated, which makes the function safe to reuse and easy to test.

3. Split deterministically

import random

def split_records(records: list[dict], valid_size: float = 0.2, seed: int = 42):
    if not 0 < valid_size < 1:
        raise ValueError("valid_size must be between 0 and 1")
    shuffled = list(records)
    random.Random(seed).shuffle(shuffled)
    cutoff = max(1, int(len(shuffled) * valid_size)) if shuffled else 0
    return shuffled[cutoff:], shuffled[:cutoff]

A fixed seed makes the split reproducible. For a real classification task, stratify by label or split by time/group. Document the choice; an unexplained split is a hidden assumption.

4. Write artifacts and a summary

import csv
from collections import Counter

def write_jsonl(path: Path, records: list[dict]) -> None:
    with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for record in records:
            handle.write(json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

def summarize(records: list[dict]) -> dict:
    return {
        "rows": len(records),
        "labels": dict(Counter(r["label"] for r in records)),
        "missing_text": sum(1 for r in records if not r["text"]),
    }

def run(raw_paths: list[Path], out_dir: Path) -> dict:
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    records = clean_records([r for path in raw_paths for r in read_jsonl(path)])
    train, valid = split_records(records)
    write_jsonl(out_dir / "train.jsonl", train)
    write_jsonl(out_dir / "valid.jsonl", valid)
    summary = {"total": summarize(records), "train": summarize(train), "valid": summarize(valid)}
    (out_dir / "summary.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(summary, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8"
    )
    return summary

The summary is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought. It lets a reviewer see row counts and label balance without opening the data.

5. Test the seams

def test_clean_drops_empty_and_duplicate():
    raw = [
        {"text": " Reset  Password ", "label": " Account "},
        {"text": "reset password", "label": "account"},
        {"text": "", "label": "bug"},
    ]
    assert clean_records(raw) == [{"text": "reset password", "label": "account"}]

def test_split_is_reproducible():
    records = [{"text": f"n{i}", "label": "a"} for i in range(10)]
    assert split_records(records, seed=7) == split_records(records, seed=7)

Test the transformations, not the whole world. A test for cleaning should not need a model or a network. A test for the split should assert determinism and disjointness.

Run it

python -m notes_pipeline.cli --raw raw/ --out data/processed/
cat data/processed/summary.json
Project connection: this is the Notes-to-Dataset Pipeline. Add the README, the CLI, the test suite and one failure analysis. The downloadable test pack defines the minimum contract.

lessons.title: Debugging and profiling AI Python
lessons.summary: Read tracebacks, add useful logs, measure time and memory, and debug API calls without guessing.
takeaways: Read a traceback from the bottom up; the last line names the exception, the frames show the path.
Log identifiers, shapes and timings, not secrets or entire prompts.
Measure before optimizing: cProfile for CPU, tracemalloc for memory, p95 latency for APIs.
lessons.practice: Reproduce one shape mismatch or KeyError from a recent script, add a log line that prints the input shape/keys before the failure, and write a regression test. Success: the next failure is obvious from the log alone.
lessons.body_html:
AI code fails in ordinary Python ways plus a few new ones: wrong tensor shapes, empty API responses, silent NaNs, and loops that look fine but take hours. Debugging is a skill you can make systematic.

Read the traceback properly

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "pipeline.py", line 42, in <module>
    train(model, data)
  File "pipeline.py", line 28, in train
    batch = next(loader)
  File "data.py", line 17, in __getitem__
    return {"input_ids": self.encodings[index]}
KeyError: 0

The last line is the actual exception; the frames above show how execution arrived there. Here the dataset has no input_ids key, or the index is wrong. Fix the contract, not the symptom.

Log the useful facts

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def train_epoch(model, loader):
    logger.info("start epoch batches=%s", len(loader))
    for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
        if step == 0:
            logger.info("first batch keys=%s shapes=%s",
                        list(batch), {k: tuple(v.shape) for k, v in batch.items()})
        ...

Log shapes, IDs, counts, durations and status codes. Do not log API keys, full documents or personal data. A good log lets you reproduce the failure without rerunning the whole pipeline.

Measure time

import time
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def timed(label):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    yield
    print(f"{label}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

with timed("load"):
    records = load_records(paths)
with timed("embed"):
    vectors = embed(records)

For a deeper look, run python -m cProfile -s cumulative script.py. Optimize the function that actually dominates the runtime, not the one that looks complicated.

Measure memory

import tracemalloc

tracemalloc.start()
records = load_records(paths)
current, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
print(f"current={current / 1e6:.1f} MB peak={peak / 1e6:.1f} MB")

Large lists of dictionaries and embeddings are common memory hogs. A generator or batch loader can keep the same pipeline within budget.

Debugging API calls

Log the request id, status, latency and a short error code — not the authorization header. Reproduce a failing call with curl or a minimal script. Check whether the failure is network, auth, rate limit, malformed output or a bad prompt. Each has a different fix.

Common AI Python errors

  • Shape mismatch — print shapes before the operation; read the expected contract.
  • NaN loss — check labels, learning rate, input scaling and empty batches.
  • KeyError in provider JSON — validate the response shape and handle missing choices.
  • Async “never awaited” — await the coroutine or run it with asyncio.run.
  • Silent NaNs in pandas — inspect isna() and dtypes before modelling.
  • Slow loop — vectorise, batch, or cache before adding hardware.
Rule: one reproducible failure, one hypothesis, one measurement. Guessing is not debugging.

lessons.title: Reproducible Python projects
lessons.summary: A project structure that another person — or future you — can run without guessing.
lessons.body_html:
An AI result is only useful if someone can reproduce it. Reproducibility is a set of small decisions: pinned dependencies, explicit configuration, fixed seeds, deterministic splits and a README that actually works.

The minimum project shape

project/
  pyproject.toml
  requirements.txt
  .env.example
  README.md
  src/project/
    config.py
    data.py
    pipeline.py
    cli.py
  tests/
    test_pipeline.py
  artifacts/          # gitignored outputs

Keep notebooks in a separate folder for exploration. The code that produces a result belongs in src/, and the code that proves it works belongs in tests/.

Configuration is an object, not scattered env reads

from dataclasses import dataclass
import os

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    data_dir: str
    model: str
    timeout: int
    seed: int

    @classmethod
    def from_env(cls):
        return cls(
            data_dir=os.environ.get("DATA_DIR", "data"),
            model=os.environ.get("LLM_MODEL", "small-model"),
            timeout=int(os.environ.get("TIMEOUT", "20")),
            seed=int(os.environ.get("SEED", "42")),
        )

One place to parse configuration means one place to test it. It also prevents hidden defaults spread across five modules.

Determinism where it matters

import random
import numpy as np

def set_seeds(seed: int) -> None:
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)

Seeds help with data splits and experimentation, but they do not make every GPU operation bit-for-bit deterministic. Record the seed, library versions and hardware when a result matters.

One command to reproduce

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env
python -m project.cli --config configs/dev.yaml
pytest -q

The README should list these exact commands, the expected outputs and one known limitation. If the setup only works on your machine, it is not a deliverable.

Rule: commit the lockfile, the config schema and the tests; do not commit the virtual environment, secrets or generated artifacts.
takeaways: Reproducibility is a design choice, not a final cleanup step.
Configuration belongs in one typed object with explicit defaults.
A README is part of the product; it must contain the exact working commands.
lessons.practice: Take an existing script and create a package with config, a CLI and one test. Delete the virtual environment and rebuild it from the README. Success: a clean run produces the same row counts.

questions.prompt: Which Python structure maps most naturally to a JSON object?
questions.explanation: JSON objects become dictionaries: keys map to strings and values map to Python objects. JSON arrays become lists.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a virtual environment?
choices: It isolates a project's interpreter and installed packages from other projects.
questions.explanation: A venv keeps dependencies isolated. Pin them in requirements or a lockfile so the environment is reproducible.

questions.prompt: Why is a vectorised NumPy operation usually better than a Python loop over a large array?
choices: It changes the data type automatically.
The operation runs in compiled code and expresses the transformation more efficiently.
It avoids the need for validation.
questions.explanation: NumPy moves the loop into compiled code. It is usually faster and clearer, though memory use still matters for very large arrays.

questions.prompt: What is a generator useful for when processing a large notes file?
choices: It loads the entire file into memory at once.
It yields one item at a time, keeping memory usage low.
questions.explanation: A generator produces values lazily. You can process a large corpus without holding every line or record in memory.

questions.prompt: An API call returns a 429 rate-limit response. What is the most reasonable handling?
choices: Retry immediately in an infinite loop.
Respect the retry guidance, use bounded exponential backoff, and surface a clear error if it persists.
Ignore the status code and parse the body.
questions.explanation: 429 is transient but must be bounded. Back off, cap attempts, and fail clearly. A tight retry loop makes the rate limit worse.

questions.prompt: You discover that a feature was computed using the full dataset mean before the train/test split. What is the problem?
choices: The test set influenced preprocessing, creating leakage and an optimistic score.
The model will train too slowly.
questions.explanation: Preprocessing statistics must be learned from the training fold only. Otherwise the validation or test set leaks into training.

flashcards.front: List vs dict vs set vs tuple?
flashcards.back: List: ordered and mutable. Dict: keyed lookup. Set: unique values. Tuple: fixed, immutable group. Choose by the behaviour you need.

flashcards.front: Why use a virtual environment for AI projects?
flashcards.back: It isolates the interpreter and dependencies, so one project's package versions do not break another. Pin dependencies for reproducibility.
flashcards.front_code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

flashcards.front: When should you use a generator?
flashcards.back: When you process a large file or corpus and do not need all items in memory at once. A generator yields one item per iteration.

flashcards.front: What should every LLM API call have?
flashcards.back: A timeout, status check, secret from the environment, explicit error handling, and a bounded retry policy only for transient failures.

flashcards.front: Why is preprocessing before a train/test split dangerous?
flashcards.back: It lets information from validation or test data influence training statistics, which is data leakage and produces optimistic evaluation.
